newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans flee crime in ever increasing numbers.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans flee crime in ever increasing numbers.

text.p: White South Africans terrified by violent crime are fleeing their country to start new lives overseas in ever increasing numbers, latest government figures showed on Tuesday.
The number of emigrants, almost all white professionals, leaving post-apartheid South Africa jumped 23.6 percent to 5,627 in the first six months of 1996 over the same time last year.
"It is still about crime. Crime is very high and even the tourists are all staying away," said Alida Casteleijn, a senior statistician with the government's Central Statistical Service.
At the same time the number of foreign newcomers willing to chance their luck on South Africa's increasingly mean streets fell -- by 4.2 percent to 2,509.

The crime wave, that sees car hijackings and murders regularly splashed across the front pages of local newspapers, has earned Johannesburg an unenviable reputation as one of the world's most dangerous cities.
Casteleijn said there was little immediate prospect of the number of emigrants falling. "I can only see that the number of people leaving will definitely rise," she said.
An entire industry of emigration consultants and international removal firms has sprung up to aid South Africans on their way.
The phenomenon has prompted calls by business-sponsored adverts for a stop to the "brain drain."
Australia is becoming an increasingly popular destination with the figures jumping from 793 in the first half of 1995 to 1,141 in the same period this year.
"People are starting to choose Australia over Britain more now, because the climate there is more comparable to our own," Casteleijn said.
The number of people leaving for Britain, still the top choice of most, rose from 1,018 to 1,288.
However, the figures do not include details of illegal immigration into the country. Most of these people are poor blacks fleeing poverty in neigbouring states such as Zimbabwe and Mozambique.
Though impossible to accurately quantify, the inflow of illegal immigrants attracted to South Africa's wealthy industries mean the country is gaining population overall, not losing it.
